Executive summary
Emerging therapeutic targets for anaemia of chronic disease (ACD) and cancer‑related anaemia (CRA) converge on the iron hormone hepcidin and the BMP/TGF‑β/SMAD axis that controls hepatocyte hepcidin, as well as erythroid signals such as erythroferrone (ERFE) that modulate iron export and availability for erythropoiesis. <cite id="4284dd1b-0">Inflammation elevates hepcidin via IL‑6/STAT3 while crosstalk with BMP/SMAD signaling integrates iron stores and demand</cite> <cite id="4284dd1b-2">with Hemojuvelin acting as a BMP co‑receptor and BMP6 as a key ligand that signals through ALK2/3 and ActRIIA/BMPRII to phosphorylate SMAD1/5/8 and regulate hepcidin transcription</cite> <cite id="4284dd1b-3">and erythropoietic demand and ERFE suppress hepcidin to facilitate iron delivery to erythropoiesis</cite>. 1) Pathophysiology and emerging biochemical targets in ACD and CRA
ACD and CRA share a common inflammatory milieu that suppresses iron availability for erythropoiesis via the iron hormone hepcidin. <cite id="4284dd1b-0">Inflammation increases hepcidin primarily through IL‑6→STAT3 signaling, while BMP/SMAD signaling is also activated and can contribute to hepcidin induction, with proposed crosstalk via inflammatory induction of activin B that signals through BMP type I/II receptors to phosphorylate SMAD1/5/8 and induce hepcidin, though in vivo contributions remain debated</cite>. <cite id="4284dd1b-2">Genetic and mechanistic data establish that HJV is a BMP co‑receptor in hepatocytes, BMP6 is essential for HJV‑mediated hepcidin regulation, and ALK3/ALK2 (type I) together with ActRIIA/BMPRII (type II) and SMAD1/5/8 are required for proper hepcidin transcription; loss of HJV/SMAD4 causes profound hepatic iron loading via depressed hepcidin</cite>. <cite id="4284dd1b-3">Erythropoietic demand and ERFE drive iron release from macrophages and hepatocytes by suppressing hepcidin during stress erythropoiesis</cite>. In cancer settings, <cite id="4284dd1b-4">tumor cytokines can oppose or modulate this axis: IL‑6 promotes hepcidin‑mediated iron restriction, whereas GDF15 is overexpressed in some cancers and suppresses hepcidin, yielding a cytokine‑dependent balance that shapes iron‑restricted anaemia</cite>. <cite id="4284dd1b-1">BMPs are recognized regulators of iron homeostasis, with BMP6 linking hepatic iron stores to hepcidin via SMAD signaling and HJV; mutations in this pathway cause human iron disorders</cite>.

Emerging molecular targets therefore include:
- Inflammatory/osteogenic branches: IL‑6/GDF15 axis and activin/ACVR1/ALK2/3 pathways that elevate hepcidin. <cite id="4284dd1b-0">Inflammatory STAT3 and SMAD signaling converge on hepcidin transcription, with activin B proposed to engage BMP/ALKs in hepatocytes</cite> <cite id="4284dd1b-2">and ALK3/ALK2/ActRIIA/BMPRII–SMAD1/5/8 signaling regulates hepcidin</cite> <cite id="4284dd1b-4">GDF15 suppresses hepcidin and is overexpressed in prostate cancer, offsetting IL‑6‑driven hepcidin elevation</cite>.
- Iron export/master regulator: hepcidin itself and its upstream sensors/signaling (HJV/BMP6/SMAD, ferroportin regulation). <cite id="4284dd1b-2">HJV/BMP6/SMAD1/5/8 control hepatic hepcidin; BMP–SMAD elements are critical in the hepcidin promoter</cite>.
- Erythroid demand/efficiency: ERFE, EPO/erythropoietic stress signaling, and pathways that enhance erythroid iron utilization. <cite id="4284dd1b-3">Erythropoietic expansion drives hepcidin suppression and iron mobilization via ERFE to support hemoglobin synthesis</cite>.
- Disease‑specific nodes: ACVR1/ALK2 in myeloproliferative neoplasms and ferroportin/FPN1 trafficking. <cite id="03ddb28f-4">ACVR1, integrated with BMP6/SMAD, regulates hepcidin; inhibition lowers hepcidin and improves anemia in myelofibrosis</cite> <cite id="03ddb28f-3">hepcidin impairs ferroportin‑1–dependent iron export in pulmonary arterial hypertension, illustrating hepcidin–FPN1 control of iron efflux</cite>.

2) How activin receptor IIA ligand traps influence iron metabolism and erythropoiesis
Activin receptor type IIA (ActRIIA) ligand traps bind and sequester multiple BMP/activin ligands, preventing activation of ALK2/3/ActRIIA/BMPRII–SMAD pathways that would otherwise elevate hepcidin and restrict iron. <cite id="03ddb28f-2">Sotatercept (ACE‑011) and luspatercept (ACE‑536) are Fc‑fused ActRIIA/ActRIIB ligand traps that bind activins, GDF8/11, and several BMPs with ligand‑dependent affinities, thereby inhibiting Smad2/3 signaling</cite>. Clinical translational signals are also encouraging. <cite id="03ddb28f-2">Sotatercept dose‑dependently stimulated hemoglobin and red blood cell parameters in healthy volunteers</cite>, and preclinical work in renal and inflammatory models <cite id="2c171edc-3">confirms rapid erythroid expansion and iron mobilization when activin signaling is blocked</cite>. Mechanistically, <cite id="4284dd1b-4">activin/ALK2/ALK3/ActRIIA–SMAD signaling increases hepcidin</cite> <cite id="03ddb28f-0">with ALK3 and ActRIIA/ActRIIB required for baseline and stimulated hepcidin expression, and BMP6 acting as a hepatic iron–responsive ligand that induces hepcidin via SMAD1/5/8</cite>; blockade upstream by ligand sequestration reduces hepcidin and enhances iron export and erythropoiesis.

Hepcidin is the rate‑limiting regulator of systemic iron export; neutralizing hepcidin raises plasma iron and promotes erythroid iron uptake, countering the iron restriction that drives ACD/CRA and ineffective erythropoiesis. <cite id="4284dd1b-3">Anemia suppresses hepcidin; inflammation elevates hepcidin, causing hypoferremia and iron‑restricted erythropoiesis</cite>. Strategies include:

- Modulating hepcidin’s upstream control: targeting HJV/BMP6/SMAD or inflammatory cytokines indirectly antagonizes hepcidin. <cite id="4284dd1b-2">BMP6–HJV–SMAD1/5/8 signaling drives hepcidin; disrupting inhibitory elements reduces hepcidin and iron overload occurs when pathologically suppressed</cite> <cite id="4284dd1b-0">and inflammation via IL‑6/STAT3 and activin/BMP SMAD cross‑talk elevates hepcidin</cite>.
- Risks: over‑antagonism can raise systemic iron and risk iron overload, particularly in chronic settings; thus, combination with erythropoietic support or inflammation control is rational. <cite id="4284dd1b-3">BMP/SMAD and erythroid signals coordinate hepcidin with iron demand; restoring iron without matching demand or failing to control inflammation can lead to dysregulation</cite>.

Therapeutic modulation includes:
- Inhibiting ALK2/ALK3/ActRIIA/ActRIIB–SMAD signaling with small molecules or ligand traps to lower hepcidin and enhance iron mobilization. <cite id="03ddb28f-4">In myelofibrosis, ACVR1 (part of BMP/activin/SMAD) drives hepcidin; pharmacologic ACVR1 inhibition (e.g., momelotinib, zilurgisertib) reduces hepcidin signaling, improving anemia with clinical approval and trial support</cite> <cite id="03ddb28f-2">and ActRIIA ligand traps broadly sequester activin/BMP ligands to suppress Smad2/3</cite>.
- Targeting inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL‑6) or tumor‑derived antagonists (e.g., GDF15) to rebalance the hepcidin axis. <cite id="4284dd1b-4">IL‑6 promotes hepcidin‑mediated iron restriction in cancer, whereas GDF15 suppresses hepcidin and is overexpressed in prostate cancer, yielding iron‑restricted anemia unless balanced</cite>.
- Preserving physiological BMP/SMAD support of erythropoiesis: certain BMP signals and endocrine factors lower hepcidin to meet demand. <cite id="4284dd1b-1">BMPs regulate hepcidin and iron metabolism; sex hormones and growth factors (EGF, HGF) can suppress hepcidin and intersect with BMP/SMAD</cite> <cite id="4284dd1b-3">erythropoietic demand and ERFE suppress hepcidin to increase iron availability for erythropoiesis</cite>.
- Disease‑specific examples: <cite id="03ddb28f-4">in myelofibrosis, ACVR1 inhibition improves anemia with regulatory approval (momelotinib) and ongoing agents (zilurgisertib) based on anemia benefits</cite>; in kidney disease models, <cite id="4284dd1b-1">BMP/SMAD signaling ties iron stores to hepcidin and therapeutic modulation is being explored</cite>.

Title: Bone Morphogenetic Proteins as Regulators of Iron Metabolism
Snippet: Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) are members of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) superfamily of signaling molecules. Mutations in certain genes influencing signaling to hepcidin via the BMP/SMAD pathway are associated with human disorders of iron metabolism, such as hereditary hemochromatosis and iron-refractory iron-deficiency anemia. Evidence suggests that signals in addition to iron stores influence hepcidin expression via the BMP/SMAD pathway. This review summarizes the details of BMP/SMAD signaling, with a particular focus on its role in iron homeostasis and iron-related diseases.

Title: Bone Morphogenetic Proteins as Regulators of Iron Metabolism
Snippet: Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) are members of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) superfamily of signaling molecules. In addition to protean roles in embryonic development, germ-line specification, and cellular differentiation, a central role in iron homeostasis has recently been demonstrated for certain BMPs. Specifically, BMP6 serves to relate hepatic iron stores to the hepatocellular expression of the iron-regulatory hormone hepcidin. This regulation occurs via cellular SMAD-signaling molecules and is strongly modulated by the BMP coreceptor hemojuvelin (HJV). Mutations in certain genes influencing signaling to hepcidin via the BMP/SMAD pathway are associated with human disorders of iron metabolism, such as hereditary hemochromatosis and iron-refractory iron-deficiency anemia. Evidence suggests that signals in addition to iron stores influence hepcidin expression via the BMP/SMAD pathway. This review summarizes the details of BMP/SMAD signaling, with a particular focus on its role in iron homeostasis and iron-related diseases.

documents.snippet: Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) are members of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) superfamily of signaling molecules. In addition to protean roles in embryonic development, germ-line specification, and cellular differentiation, a central role in iron homeostasis has recently been demonstrated for certain BMPs. Specifically, BMP6 serves to relate hepatic iron stores to the hepatocellular expression of the iron-regulatory hormone hepcidin. This regulation occurs via cellular SMAD-signaling molecules and is strongly modulated by the BMP coreceptor hemojuvelin (HJV). Mutations in certain genes influencing signaling to hepcidin via the BMP/SMAD pathway are associated with human disorders of iron metabolism, such as hereditary hemochromatosis and iron-refractory iron-deficiency anemia. Evidence suggests that signals in addition to iron stores influence hepcidin expression via the BMP/SMAD pathway. This review summarizes the details of BMP/SMAD signaling, with a particular focus on its role in iron homeostasis and iron-related diseases.

Misregulation of the activin pathway has been implicated in anemia, myeloma-associated osteolysis, metastatic bone disease, and carcinogenesis. 25 Activin and activin receptors, because of their diverse biological processes, have been extensively studied as potential therapeutic targets in several pathological conditions. 26 In particular, the inhibition of the TGF-β pathway is the mechanism by which a therapeutic effect can be achieved, acting on the Smad2/3 cascade. Two such agents are Sotatercept (ACE-011) and Luspatercept (ACE-536), ligandtrapping fusion proteins containing the modified extracellular domain of activin receptor type IIA (ActRIIA) or IIB (ActRIIB), respectively, fused to the Fc domain of IgG1. 27,28 Both of them sequestrate the ligand before it can interact with the receptor, thus inhibiting the signal transduction cascade. It has been demonstrated that in ex vivo conditions, ACE-011 binds Activin A and B, GDF8, GDF11, and other BMPs (such as BMP6, BMP7, and BMP10) with different affinities. 27 Luspatercept, on the other hand, has shown high binding capacity with activin B, GDF8, and GDF11, but not with Activin A. 28,32 Both of them do not interact with TGF-β1, TGF-β2 nor TGF-β1. These activin ligand traps show similar binding ligand-binding profiles, but ACE-536 shows a higher ligand selectivity making this specific molecule more suitable for treating anemia and ineffective erythropoiesis.

Summary
Inflammation-driven anemias (anaemia of chronic disease and cancer‑related anemia) raise hepcidin via a common TGF‑β/BMP/SMAD pathway that is overlaid by cytokine networks; both “activin receptor IIA ligand traps” (extracellular decoy sequestration) and intracellular BMP/SMAD modulators suppress hepcidin by converging on the same hepatocyte HAMP transcriptional node, thereby restoring iron release and hemoglobinization. <cite id="7c3b7790-4">Activin B produced by endothelial and Kupffer cells during LPS‑stimulated inflammation signals through ALK2 in concert with ActRIIA to phosphorylate BR‑Smads and stimulate hepcidin transcription in hepatocytes</cite> and <cite id="519e0e4a-0">BMP/SMAD pathway components, including SMAD1/5/8, are required for maximal hepcidin induction by inflammatory cytokines</cite>. <cite id="519e0e4a-2">In the liver, overexpressing inhibitory modulators (SMAD6, BAMBI, Follistatin) reduces hepcidin by acting at ligand, receptor, and intracellular SMAD levels, respectively</cite>, while <cite id="519e0e4a-4">in vivo inhibition of ALK2/ALK3 suppresses hepcidin in mouse models of anemia of inflammation</cite>. Together, these mechanisms point to a shared downstream regulatory node at the HAMP locus, where activin‑driven BR‑SMAD and cytokine‑driven AR‑SMAD/STAT3 converge and are counter‑regulated by intracellular BMP antagonists and coaggregators such as HSPGs. <cite id="519e0e4a-0">Intact SMAD1/5/8 function is required for full IL‑6/STAT3 induction of hepcidin, and activin B can activate SMAD1/5/8 via ALK2/ALK3</cite>, and <cite id="519e0e4a-4">heparan sulfate proteoglycans are essential coregulators that scaffold both BMP/SMAD and IL‑6/STAT3 to the hepcidin promoter</cite>.

Background: Hepcidin control and the inflammatory override
Basal hepcidin responds to iron by BMP ligands (BMP2/6) that bind HSPGs, HJV, and BMPRs on hepatocytes to phosphorylate SMAD1/5/8, which cooperate with SMAD4 to activate the HAMP promoter; inflammatory cytokines add parallel and convergent pathways. <cite id="519e0e4a-4">HSPGs are upstream coregulators: their loss sharply attenuates BMP6‑ and IL‑6‑stimulated hepcidin, with systemic iron redistribution</cite>. <cite id="519e0e4a-0">IL‑6/JAK/STAT3 engages a STAT3 element in the hepcidin promoter and requires an intact BMP‑responsive element for maximal induction, indicating functional interdependence of IL‑6/STAT3 and BMP/SMAD pathways</cite>. <cite id="519e0e4a-0">Activin B acts as a surrogate BMP‑family ligand that promotes hepcidin via SMAD1/5/8 phosphorylation and crosstalks between IL‑6/STAT3 and BMP/SMAD</cite>.

Activin receptor IIA ligand-trap mechanism in CAD and cancer‑related anemia
Anemia of chronic disease and cancer‑related anemia share a key inflammatory lesion: increased activin B production by sinusoidal and parenchymal cells that signals through ALK2/ActRIIA to BR‑SMADs, inducing HAMP. <cite id="7c3b7790-4">Endothelial cells and Kupffer cells produce activin B during LPS‑induced inflammation, and ALK2 with ActRIIA transmits the activin B signal to stimulate hepcidin transcription via phosphorylation and activation of BR‑Smad in hepatocytes</cite>. <cite id="519e0e4a-0">Activin B promotes hepcidin by stimulating SMAD1/5/8 phosphorylation through interactions with ActR2A, ALK2, and ALK3</cite>. Extracellular “ligand traps” that present the Type IIA receptor ectodomain (e.g., ActRIIA‑Fc or ALK2/ALK3‑Fc) sequester activin ligands and block productive signaling to hepatocytes, thereby lowering hepcidin. <cite id="519e0e4a-0">ALK3‑Fc and related ligand‑trap constructs can reduce hepcidin expression in hepatocytes treated with activin B by preventing ligand engagement of ALK3; mechanistically, this is consistent with a broader role for ALK2/ActRIIA‑mediated sequestration in inflammation‑induced hepcidin</cite>. <cite id="67808d15-1">ALK3‑Fc decreased hepcidin expression in hepatocytes exposed to activin B, consistent with a model where ALK2/ActRIIA complexes mediate activin B signal transmission to BR‑Smads in vivo</cite>. <cite id="67808d15-3">Pharmacologic inhibition of ALK2/ALK3/ALK6 (e.g., LDN‑193189) suppresses BR‑Smad–mediated hepcidin expression in animal models of anemia of inflammation</cite>. Thus, activin receptor IIA ligand traps act at the ligand‑receptor interface to relieve BR‑SMAD pressure on the HAMP enhancer and restore iron mobilization.

Intracellular BMP/SMAD modulators that converge on the same HAMP node
Multiple intracellular layers of BMP/SMAD regulation can suppress hepcidin by converging on the same HAMP locus, providing complementary strategies to counter inflammatory hepcidin elevation:

- Extracellular/inhibitory ligand antagonists: <cite id="519e0e4a-2">Overexpressing follistatin in hepatocytes suppresses hepcidin, acting at the ligand level</cite>. <cite id="519e0e4a-0">SMAD6 and BAMBI are controlled by BMP/SMAD signaling but are not downregulated by iron, suggesting they can buffer pathway activity when endogenous SMAD7 is limited</cite>.

- Membrane receptor antagonism: <cite id="519e0e4a-2">BAMBI overexpression reduces hepcidin and abrogates BMP6‑induced hepcidin, consistent with a dominant‑negative blockade of BMP receptor activation</cite>.

- Intracellular SMAD antagonism: <cite id="519e0e4a-2">SMAD6 overexpression decreases phosphorylated SMAD1/5/8 and hepcidin mRNA, demonstrating inhibition of intracellular SMAD phosphorylation</cite>. <cite id="519e0e4a-3">In Huh7 cells, SMAD6, BAMBI, and Follistatin co‑reducing hepcidin even in the presence of BMP6 indicate distinct but overlapping control points: folllistatin (ligand), BAMBI (receptor), and SMAD6 (SMAD), with partial functional replacement for SMAD7</cite>.

- Pathway‑level dominance and crosstalk: <cite id="519e0e4a-0">Intact SMAD1/5/8 signaling is required for maximal IL‑6/STAT3‑mediated hepcidin induction, and activin B can activate SMAD1/5/8 via ALK2/ALK3</cite>. This places the HAMP enhancer under dual control: cytokine STAT complexes cooperate with SMAD1/5/8, and intracellular modulators (SMAD6/7, BAMBI) blunt this axis from within the cell.

Mechanistic convergence at the HAMP enhancer: SMADs, HSPGs, STAT3/IRF1, and crosstalk
Evidence converges on a single enhancer‑promoter module in HAMP where multiple TGF‑β/BMP/activin branches and cytokine pathways integrate:

- Scaffolded co‑localization: <cite id="519e0e4a-4">HSPGs on liver sinusoidal and parenchymal cells are essential co‑coregulators that assemble BMP/SMAD complexes and IL‑6/STAT3 at the hepcidin promoter; genetic attenuation of HSPG biosynthesis or sulfation sharply reduces both BMP6‑ and IL‑6‑stimulated hepcidin</cite>. <cite id="519e0e4a-0">Activin B uses BMP type I receptors (ALK3/ALK2) with Type IIA receptors (ACVR2A/2B) to activate SMAD1/5/8 and induce hepcidin</cite>.

- Shared SMAD logic: <cite id="7c3b7790-4">Activin B engages ALK2–ActRIIA to drive BR‑SMAD phosphorylation and HAMP transcription</cite>, while <cite id="519e0e4a-0">AR‑SMAD signaling via ALK4/ActRIIs and ALK3/ALK2 can be activated by activin B and BMPs respectively, with BR‑SMAD signaling specifically linked to hepcidin</cite>. <cite id="519e0e4a-0">The IL‑6/STAT3 pathway activates a STAT3 response element in the HAMP promoter, but maximal induction requires the BMP response element and intact SMAD1/5/8 function, evidencing convergence at the HAMP enhancer</cite>.

- Intracellular antagonists at the node: <cite id="519e0e4a-2">Hepatic Smad7 loss increases phospho‑SMAD1/5/8 and hepcidin; conversely, overexpressing SMAD6, BAMBI, or Follistatin reduces hepcidin by inhibiting ligand availability, receptor activation, or intracellular SMAD phosphorylation, respectively</cite>. <cite id="519e0e4a-0">SMAD6 and BAMBI are regulated by BMP/SMAD and can partially substitute for SMAD7 under certain conditions, indicating a hierarchy of intracellular checkpoints that converge on the same HAMP locus</cite>.

- Cancer‑specific cytokine overlays: Tumor microenvironments elevate IL‑6/STAT3 and produce TGF‑β/BMP agonists and antagonists, reinforcing hepcidin via the same HAMP node. <cite id="519e0e4a-0">BMP6 and iron increase matriptase‑2 (TMPRSS6) indirectly, but inflammation‑driven IL‑6/STAT3 directly upregulates hepcidin and critically depends on intact SMAD signaling</cite>. <cite id="519e0e4a-0">Activin B may be a key mediator linking infection/inflammation and cancer to hepcidin via its ability to activate SMAD1/5/8 through ALK2/ALK3</cite>.

Putting CAD and cancer‑related anemia on the same mechanistic footing
Across chronic inflammatory liver disease and cancer‑related anemia, inflammation elevates hepcidin through cytokine‑driven IL‑6/STAT3 and activin‑driven BR‑SMAD signaling that share the HAMP enhancer. <cite id="7c3b7790-4">Sinusoidal and parenchymal cytokine sources produce activin B that drives hepatocyte BR‑SMAD activation and HAMP transcription</cite>, while <cite id="519e0e4a-0">inflammatory IL‑6/STAT3 upregulates hepcidin but requires a functional BMP/SMAD module</cite>. In both settings, activin receptor IIA ligand traps (e.g., ActRIIA‑Fc/ALK2‑Fc) and intracellular SMAD modulators (SMAD7 restoration, SMAD6/BAMBI/follistatin) converge by attenuating ligand engagement or intracellular SMAD phosphorylation at the HAMP locus, thereby reducing hepcidin and improving iron availability. <cite id="67808d15-3">ALK2/ALK3 inhibition suppresses hepcidin in anemia of inflammation</cite>, and <cite id="519e0e4a-2">overexpression of SMAD6, BAMBI, or Follistatin reduces hepcidin in hepatocytes and in vivo</cite>.

Therapeutic implications and convergence points
- Extracellular strategies: <cite id="67808d15-3">ALK2/ALK3 inhibitors</cite> and <cite id="7c3b7790-4">ActRIIA‑mediated signaling blockade via ALK2–ActRIIA complexes</cite> lower BR‑SMAD pressure on HAMP.
- Intracellular strategies: <cite id="519e0e4a-2">SMAD7 replacement therapy, SMAD6/BAMBI overexpression, and follistatin augmentation</cite> dampen pathway flux at receptor and SMAD levels.
- Upstream scaffolding: <cite id="519e0e4a-4">Targeting HSPGs reduces hepcidin by disrupting the assembly of BMP/SMAD and IL‑6/STAT3 complexes at the enhancer</cite>.
These approaches point to the HAMP enhancer as the final common node integrating activin/BMP/STAT/IRF signals and serving as the principal therapeutic lever in CAD and cancer‑related anemia.

Title: Regulation of hepcidin expression by inflammation-induced activin B
Snippet: Previously, activin B was thought to be induced in response to hepatic inflammation, and the induced activin B stimulated the expression of the iron-regulating hormone hepcidin 19,21 . However, the source of activin B and the detailed induction of hepcidin were unclear. Here, we clarify the signal transduction from sinusoids to parenchyma that is mediated by activin B in response to liver inflammation. Endothelial cells and Kupffer cells produce activin B during LPS-induced inflammation, and the induced activin B stimulates hepcidin production in liver parenchymal cells. ALK2 in concert with ActRIIA transmits the activin B signal to stimulate hepcidin transcription through phosphorylation and activation of BR-Smad. Activin B also stimulates AR-Smad-mediated signaling through ALK4 and ActRIIs, leading to up-regulation of CTGF expression (Supplementary Fig. S9). 

Previous studies have reported that hepcidin transcription is regulated by activin B, but conflicting mechanisms were proposed 19,21 . Besson-Fournier et al. 19 suggested ALK3 is the primary receptor that induces hepcidin transcription through activin B, whereas ALK2 was proposed to be the main receptor to confer activin B-induced hepcidin transcription 21 . The present results on the transcriptional regulation of hepcidin by activin B are consistent with the results of Canali et al. 21 . It is unclear why the previous results are inconsistent. Besson-Fournier et al. 19 concluded that ALK3 transmits activin B-induced hepcidin expression because treatment with the extracellular region of ALK3 fused to an immunoglobulin Fc domain (ALK3-Fc) but not ALK2-Fc decreased the hepcidin expression level in hepatocytes treated with activin B. The interpretation was that activin B was trapped by ALK3-Fc and could not be bound to ALK3 expressed at the cell surface.

Snippet: In this issue of Blood Advances, Leal et al 1 identify halofuginone as a suppressor of the iron-regulatory hormone, hepcidin, through a heparan sulfate-dependent mechanism. Hepcidin, a liver-derived peptide hormone, restricts systemic iron availability by binding ferroportin and triggering its degradation. 2 Upstream positive modulators of hepcidin expression include iron itself and inflammation. A critical upstream regulator of both pathways is the hepatic HSPG network. HSPGs are cell-surface glycoproteins bearing sulfated heparan sulfate chains that scaffold ligand-receptor complexes across many signaling systems. 3 In prior work, the authors demonstrated that hepatic HSPGs are essential coregulators of BMP/SMAD-driven hepcidin synthesis: genetic inactivation of heparan sulfate biosynthesis or reduction of heparan sulfate sulfation sharply attenuates both BMP6-and IL-6-stimulated hepcidin and causes systemic iron redistribution in mice. 4

Title: Regulation of hepcidin expression by inflammation-induced activin B
Snippet: Previously, activin B was thought to be induced in response to hepatic inflammation, and the induced activin B stimulated the expression of the iron-regulating hormone hepcidin 19,21 . However, the source of activin B and the detailed induction of hepcidin were unclear. Here, we clarify the signal transduction from sinusoids to parenchyma that is mediated by activin B in response to liver inflammation. Endothelial cells and Kupffer cells produce activin B during LPS-induced inflammation, and the induced activin B stimulates hepcidin production in liver parenchymal cells. ALK2 in concert with ActRIIA transmits the activin B signal to stimulate hepcidin transcription through phosphorylation and activation of BR-Smad. Activin B also stimulates AR-Smad-mediated signaling through ALK4 and ActRIIs, leading to up-regulation of CTGF expression (Supplementary Fig. S9). 

Previous studies have reported that hepcidin transcription is regulated by activin B, but conflicting mechanisms were proposed 19,21 . Besson-Fournier et al. 19 suggested ALK3 is the primary receptor that induces hepcidin transcription through activin B, whereas ALK2 was proposed to be the main receptor to confer activin B-induced hepcidin transcription 21 . The present results on the transcriptional regulation of hepcidin by activin B are consistent with the results of Canali et al. 21 . It is unclear why the previous results are inconsistent. Besson-Fournier et al. 19 concluded that ALK3 transmits activin B-induced hepcidin expression because treatment with the extracellular region of ALK3 fused to an immunoglobulin Fc domain (ALK3-Fc) but not ALK2-Fc decreased the hepcidin expression level in hepatocytes treated with activin B. The interpretation was that activin B was trapped by ALK3-Fc and could not be bound to ALK3 expressed at the cell surface.
